I think that they genuinely are aiming to take jobs with this technology. If/when robotaxis become ubiquitous, driving may no longer be an employment option. A lot of the mundane tasks that frequently get outsourced are also in the cross hairs. If they haven't already done it, they are actively trying to eliminate many of those positions. Even for jobs that will continue to need human input, with a significant increase in efficiency there will be a decrease in demand. I know that you address this in the video, but if the number of tellers expanded because they took on additional responsibilities, the roles that previously handled those responsibilities likely shrunk. Also, from a pure free market perspective, the fact that the steady rise in efficiency has coincided with a rise in wage inequality might suggest that it has contributed to a shift in labor market dynamics, reducing the demand for labor, right?

You're missing something important. You're thinking "it'll do this task or that task." What happens when it will do all the tasks? "Hey, Claude, make me a video about how AI isn't going to take jobs." Boom. Done. We're not talking about losing the guys who made buggy whips or elevator operators. We're seriously talking about AI replacing writers, artists, musicians, doctors (probably not surgeons, but a lot of others), lawyers, accountants, programmers .... Decades before ChatGPT, people in my field were promising to build a computer program that would do my job. My job is essentially 4 tasks. If the computer can do 3 (it's nearly there), they'll outsource the 4th to someone else -- it'll be one more task they have to do. At best, in a department that needs 10 of me now, they'll need 2 in a few years. But AI fans just keep promising that somehow other jobs will come out of the ether and replace the ones we lose. No. Every knowledge worker's job is on the chopping block. Every creative is at risk. Blue collar work? They're trying hard to automate those, too. GM replaces a few more workers with a robot every year. Amazon's doing the same. We'll be left with a service economy where almost no one has the money to pay for any services. Think Ready Player One's multi-level trailer parks where everyone lives on welfare except the blessed few who managed to have a job with one of the computer corporations.

I've been personally working with AI every day for over a year. Investigating and testing it's capabilities. Monitoring the way it "thinks". Installing harnesses and configuring, testing and improving them. AI is not what they tell you it is. To me, AI doesn't stand for Artificial Intelligence, because it's not "intelligent". It really stands for Automated Inference. So it's very limited in what it can do on its own. It needs humans to meticulously curate it's instructions and loops. It needs a human to refine, tweak, adjust and shift it's operating instructions so it gets things right. Granted, you can totally use AI to do this, but it can't do it on it's own and it never will in it's current state. Now if they integrate it with human brain tissue, that's a different story. They're experimenting with that already. They have been for about a decade at least. I don't think they will tell you if they're doing that but we'll eventually be able to tell as long as we stay vigilant and monitor its behavior. I wouldn't worry too much and I would definitely try to learn as much about it as you can so you can remain grounded in reality of how it really works.
